items.title: The Two-Speed Mind
items.question: Which psychologist's research gave us fast intuition versus slow reasoning as two systems of thought?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Daniel Kahneman, with Amos Tversky, mapped the fast and slow modes.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Kahneman. Daniel Kahneman's decades of experiments with Amos Tversky became 'Thinking, Fast and Slow'. Their partnership — one psychologist, one mathematical mind — earned a Nobel Prize in economics.
items.lessonContent:
Dual-process theory splits thinking into fast intuition and slow deliberation.
The fast mode handles most of life brilliantly — and fails predictably at statistics.
The slow mode checks the work, but only when it is invited and energized.
Noticing which mode is driving is itself a trainable skill.
Share this: catch one instant answer today and redo it slowly, then compare.

items.title: The Obedience Lab
items.question: Whose 1960s experiments showed ordinary volunteers delivering apparent electric shocks on an authority's orders?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Stanley Milgram's Yale obedience studies, the most debated experiments in psychology.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Milgram. Stanley Milgram's volunteers delivered what they believed were dangerous shocks when a calm experimenter said continue. About two-thirds went to maximum voltage — a finding about ordinary people, not monsters.
items.lessonContent:
Authority plus distance plus polite persistence moves ordinary people far.
The studies were designed after the war to understand how bureaucracies recruit decency.
Proximity to the victim cut obedience sharply — closeness is the antidote.
Modern ethics boards would never approve the original design.
Share this: notice one instruction today you'd refuse only if you looked the affected person in the eye.

items.title: Lines on a Card
items.question: Whose conformity experiments had volunteers give wrong answers about simple line lengths after hearing a unanimous wrong majority?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Solomon Asch's line-judgement studies on the power of unanimous majorities.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Asch. Solomon Asch showed volunteers cards with obvious line lengths, seeded the room with confederates giving wrong answers, and watched about a third of real responses bend. One visible dissenter restored most independence.
items.lessonContent:
Unanimity is the active ingredient — one ally collapses most conformity pressure.
The task must be easy enough that error is otherwise near zero, isolating the social force.
Public statements shift; private ballots stay put.
Juries and panels are designed around exactly this finding.
Share this: in your next group call, be the first dissent and watch the room exhale.

items.title: The Mock Prison
items.question: Whose 1971 Stanford experiment assigned students to guard and prisoner roles, then watched the roles consume them?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Philip Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, halted after six days.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Zimbardo. Philip Zimbardo's basement mock-prison spiralled so fast that the two-week study was stopped on day six. Later scholarship complicates the story — guards were coached — but the lesson about situations over dispositions survives in subtler form.
items.lessonContent:
Situations shape behaviour more than personalities do — roles recruit their players fast.
The study was stopped early when guards' cruelty escalated beyond the plan.
Later archives revealed coaching, complicating the clean narrative.
The honest takeaway survives revision: design the situation, and you design much of the behaviour.
Share this: audit one toxic routine in your life for the situation sustaining it.

items.title: Dogs That Learned
items.question: Which physiologist's salivating dogs founded the study of conditioned reflexes?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Ivan Pavlov: bells, food, and the birth of classical conditioning.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Pavlov. Ivan Pavlov noticed his lab dogs salivating at the sight of assistants, then showed that any neutral signal paired with food becomes a trigger. Conditioning that automatic is now the backbone of phobia therapy and animal training alike.
items.lessonContent:
Classical conditioning pairs a neutral signal with a reflex until the signal alone suffices.
The mechanism needs no thought — it runs in sea slugs and humans alike.
Extinction works the same machinery in reverse: unpair, and the response fades.
Advertising is applied conditioning at industrial scale.
Share this: notice one jingle-to-craving link in yourself today and name its pairing history.

items.title: The Dissonant Cult
items.question: Which psychologist studied a doomsday cult whose failed prophecy made members believe more strongly?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Leon Festinger, founder of cognitive dissonance theory.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Festinger. Leon Festinger infiltrated the cult with colleagues and watched failed prophecy convert into fervent proselytizing — dissonance resolved by doubling down. The book 'When Prophecy Fails' remains the founding case study.
items.lessonContent:
Dissonance theory: contradictions between action and belief resolve in belief's favour.
Failed prophecies often strengthen movements — the invested double down.
Post-purchase rationalization is the same machinery in daily dress.
Noticing your own rationalization in real time is genuinely difficult.
Share this: catch one explanation you invented after the fact today and label it.

items.title: Smoke in the Room
items.question: Which pair of psychologists ran the smoke-filled-room experiment proving crowds inhibit helping?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Darley and Latané, whose bystander research began with the Kitty Genovese case.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Darley and Latané. John Darley and Bibb Latané filled a room with smoke while confederates ignored it — lone subjects reported the smoke, grouped ones sat in it. Their bystander research rebuilt emergency training around naming individuals.
items.lessonContent:
Diffusion of responsibility: each witness assumes another will act, so nobody does.
Pluralistic ignorance compounds it — calm faces all around read as evidence of calm.
Naming one specific person collapses both effects at once.
Emergency protocols now drill the pointed finger, not the general alarm.
Share this: tell someone tonight to point at one person, not shout at a crowd.

items.title: The Marshmallow Wait
items.question: Whose 1970s Stanford experiments tested children's ability to delay gratification with a single treat?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Walter Mischel's marshmallow studies on self-control.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Mischel. Walter Mischel offered children one treat now or two for waiting — and the waiters' strategies (looking away, singing) mattered as much as willpower. The long-term correlations launched decades of debate about trust, background and temperament.
items.lessonContent:
Delay of gratification is partly strategy, not raw will — look-away tactics beat white-knuckling.
Later replications showed family background carries much of the predictive power.
A child's waiting also measures trust that the promised second treat will actually arrive.
Self-control turns out to be situational as much as personal.
Share this: test your own delay tonight on dessert, with a look-away strategy ready.

items.title: The Pyramid of Needs
items.question: Whose hierarchy arranges human needs from food and safety up to self-actualization?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Abraham Maslow's pyramid, from physiology at the base to self-actualization at the peak.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Maslow. Abraham Maslow proposed that lower needs must be substantially met before higher ones motivate — hunger before belonging, belonging before esteem. Critics note the order flexes across cultures, but the ladder remains psychology's most famous diagram.
items.lessonContent:
The hierarchy orders needs: body, safety, belonging, esteem, then self-actualization.
Lower levels demand satisfaction before higher ones fully motivate.
Critics rightly note cultural variation in the ordering.
As a diagnostic of what is missing in a life, it still works beautifully.
Share this: map your own current week onto the pyramid tonight and find the loudest level.

items.title: Interpreter of Dreams
items.question: Which founder of psychoanalysis wrote 'The Interpretation of Dreams'?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Sigmund Freud, who made dreams the royal road to the unconscious.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Freud. Sigmund Freud's 1900 masterwork argued dreams disguise forbidden wishes, launching psychoanalysis as a movement. Modern sleep science keeps the observation that dreams matter while discarding most of his decodings.
items.lessonContent:
Psychoanalysis proposed that dreams disguise wishes the waking mind rejects.
Free association, slips and jokes became its evidence-gathering tools.
Modern psychology keeps little of the theory but owes it the talking cure itself.
The unconscious, however renamed, survived every revision.
Share this: write one recent dream down tonight before the censor wakes up too.

items.title: Archetype Hunter
items.question: Which psychologist split from Freud and proposed the collective unconscious full of archetypes?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Carl Jung: archetypes, the collective unconscious, and introversion versus extraversion.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Jung. Carl Jung broke with Freud to argue for inherited, universal patterns — hero, shadow, trickster — living in a collective unconscious. He also gave everyday language the words introvert and extravert.
items.lessonContent:
Jung's archetypes are recurring mythic patterns: hero, shadow, trickster, wise elder.
Introversion and extraversion entered everyday speech from his typology.
The collective unconscious claims some patterns are inherited, not learned.
Storytellers mine the archetypes deliberately — Joseph Campbell built a career on them.
Share this: cast tonight's film in archetypes and watch the plot explain itself.

items.title: Rewards and Punishments
items.question: Who studied learning through rewards and punishments using pigeons and rats in controlled boxes?
items.correctExplanation: Right — B. F. Skinner, the radical behaviorist who shaped behaviour with reinforcement schedules.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Skinner. His experiments showed that reward timing shapes behaviour more than reward size — unpredictable rewards addict fastest, which is the schedule casinos run on. He treated minds as black boxes and changed education, parenting and animal training regardless.
items.lessonContent:
Operant conditioning: behaviour followed by reward repeats; followed by cost, it fades.
Variable-ratio schedules addict hardest — unpredictable wins beat steady ones.
Slot machines are Skinner boxes with better lighting.
The framework works whether or not you believe minds do anything inside.
Share this: spot one variable reward in your own apps tonight and name its schedule.

items.title: Learned Optimism
items.question: Which psychologist studied learned helplessness in dogs and later founded positive psychology?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Martin Seligman: from helpless dogs to the science of flourishing.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Seligman. Martin Seligman discovered that dogs subjected to inescapable shocks stop trying to escape — learned helplessness — then spent his later career founding positive psychology, the study of what makes life worth living. Explanatory style turned out to be the bridge.
items.lessonContent:
Learned helplessness: uncontrollable shocks teach passivity that outlasts the shocks.
Explanatory style — how you narrate setbacks — predicts who stays helpless.
Positive psychology then asked the inverted question: what builds flourishing?
Gratitude visits and strengths-spotting are its most replicated tools.
Share this: rewrite one setback tonight in the permanent-versus-temporary frame and feel the difference.

items.title: Growth versus Fixed
items.question: Whose research distinguishes a growth mindset from a fixed mindset in learners?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Carol Dweck: believing ability grows changes how effort, failure and feedback work.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Dweck. Carol Dweck showed that students who believe intelligence can grow persist longer, enjoy challenge more, and recover from failure faster. Praising effort over talent nudges the belief; praising talent nudges the fixed trap.
items.lessonContent:
Growth mindset: ability as expandable through effort and strategy.
Fixed mindset: ability as a fixed quantity to be proven again and again.
The same failure teaches one student and defines another — the belief decides.
Praise effort and process, not talent, to install the growth frame.
Share this: rephrase one compliment you give tonight from talent to process.

items.title: The Nudge Unit
items.question: Which economist won a Nobel for showing that small choice-architecture tweaks steer behaviour better than mandates?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Richard Thaler, father of nudge theory and behavioural economics' bridge into policy.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Thaler. Richard Thaler showed that defaults, framing and friction steer choices more cheaply than rules — organ-donor defaults and retirement auto-enrollment moved millions. Governments now run nudge units on exactly this insight.
items.lessonContent:
Nudges preserve freedom while steering: defaults, framing and friction do the quiet work.
Auto-enrolled pensions beat exhortation campaigns at trivial cost.
Choice architecture is unavoidable — every menu nudges — so design it deliberately.
Libertarian paternalism is the philosophy: free to choose, guided toward better.
Share this: set one default in your own life tonight so future-you chooses well by inertia.

items.title: Predictably Irrational
items.question: Which behavioural economist wrote 'Predictably Irrational' about the systematic ways decisions go wrong?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Dan Ariely: free chocolate, decoy pricing, and the anatomy of everyday irrationality.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Ariely. Dan Ariely's experiments — the Economist subscription decoy, the pain of paying, cheating studies — showed irrationality with patterns, hence predictable. His own burn injuries turned him toward studying suffering and decisions.
items.lessonContent:
Behavioural economics maps systematic irrationality: decoys, anchors, free-zero effects.
The mistakes are predictable, which makes them designable-around.
Decoy pricing steers choices without changing any option's merits.
Knowing the catalogue converts manipulation into amusement.
Share this: spot one decoy price on your next shopping trip and admire the machinery.

items.title: The Paradox of Choice
items.question: Which psychologist argued that too many options paralyse decisions and shrink satisfaction?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Barry Schwartz, who showed abundance can tyrannize rather than liberate.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Schwartz. Barry Schwartz's jam study — 24 flavours drawing crowds, 6 flavours selling — became the icon of choice overload. Maximizers, who must pick best, suffer most; satisficers, who pick good-enough, stay happier.
items.lessonContent:
Choice overload: beyond a handful of options, deferral rises and satisfaction falls.
Maximizers hunt the best and drown in comparisons; satisficers settle and stay happier.
Regret grows with forgone alternatives — every extra option is a future second-guess.
Curation is a kindness: good defaults beat infinite shelves.
Share this: shop from three pre-chosen options tonight instead of scrolling everything.

items.title: Mere Exposure
items.question: Which psychologist showed that simply seeing something repeatedly makes people like it more?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Robert Zajonc's mere-exposure effect: familiarity breeds fondness.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Zajonc. Robert Zajonc flashed images, sounds and symbols at subjects and watched liking rise with repetition — no interaction, no merit, just exposure. Advertising runs on exactly this: the tenth viewing converts the first nine's indifference.
items.lessonContent:
Mere exposure: repeated neutral contact raises liking — familiarity is fondness's raw material.
The effect needs no reasons and survives subliminal presentation.
Pop songs grow on you by the same machinery as propaganda.
Novelty-seekers should know their tastes are partly a replay count.
Share this: notice one song, brand or face you like now that bored you at first sight.

items.title: Halo's First Light
items.question: Which early psychologist named the halo effect, where one trait colours judgements of unrelated ones?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Edward Thorndike, who spotted officers' ratings glowing with unwarranted consistency.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Thorndike. Edward Thorndike found military raters scoring the same soldier consistently high or low across unrelated traits — the glow spread. He named it the halo effect, and a century of interviews, trials and elections has confirmed the shine.
items.lessonContent:
The halo effect: one admired trait inflates ratings of unrelated traits.
Thorndike found it in officers' fitness ratings — consistent glow across categories.
Attractive defendants receive lighter sentences; taller candidates win more votes.
Structured scoring, trait by trait, is the practical defence.
Share this: audit one judgement you made about a person and split the traits honestly.

items.title: Little Albert
items.question: Which behaviourist conditioned a baby to fear a white rat by pairing it with loud noises?
items.correctExplanation: Right — John B. Watson's Little Albert study, conditioning's most infamous demonstration.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Watson. John Watson paired a loud clang with a white rat until the infant feared the rat — and rabbits, fur coats and Santa beards by generalization. Modern ethics would never permit it; modern therapy still uses its machinery in reverse.
items.lessonContent:
Little Albert: pairing a neutral object with fright manufactured a phobia on schedule.
Generalization spread the fear to rabbits, fur and beards.
Systematic desensitization runs the machinery backwards to cure phobias.
The study's ethics horrify today — no consent, no debrief, no follow-up care.
Share this: trace one of your own irrational flinches to its original pairing.

items.title: The Doll Studies
items.question: Whose Bobo-doll experiments showed children imitating adults' aggression toward toys?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Albert Bandura: children who watched aggression performed it, hammer for hammer.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Bandura. Albert Bandura's nursery studies showed children copying exactly the punches they had watched adults deliver to the Bobo doll. Observational learning entered psychology — and the debate over screen violence — through that playroom door.
items.lessonContent:
Observational learning: watched behaviour becomes performed behaviour, hammer for hammer.
Bandura's Bobo studies founded social learning theory on nursery footage.
Self-efficacy — belief in your own capability — grew from the same research program.
The screen-violence debate has cited these dolls ever since.
Share this: notice one habit you caught purely by watching someone you admire.

items.title: Stages of Right
items.question: Whose theory arranges moral reasoning into stages from punishment-avoidance up to universal principles?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Lawrence Kohlberg's stages of moral development, from obedience to principled conscience.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Kohlberg. Lawrence Kohlberg posed dilemmas like the runaway trolley of medicine — a husband stealing a drug — and scored the reasoning, not the verdict. Higher stages invoke principles that can overrule law itself.
items.lessonContent:
Kohlberg's stages climb from punishment-avoidance through conformity to universal principles.
The dilemmas (a stolen drug for a dying wife) test reasoning, never answers.
Real people reason across stages depending on domain and stakes.
Gilligan's critique added care ethics to a justice-heavy ladder.
Share this: ask someone why stealing medicine might be right — then grade the reasoning, not the verdict.

items.title: The Hammer Philosopher
items.question: Which philosopher declared 'God is dead' and wrote of the Übermensch and eternal recurrence?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — Friedrich Nietzsche, philosophy's hammer, diagnosing a civilization that had killed its own foundations.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Nietzsche. Friedrich Nietzsche announced God's death as a cultural event to be faced, proposed the Übermensch as self-overcoming, and tested readers with eternal recurrence — would you relive this exact life forever? Misuse by later regimes distorts a thinker who despised them in print.
items.lessonContent:
'God is dead' diagnoses a culture, not a deity — the foundations collapsed, the building stands by habit.
The Übermensch answers with self-overcoming: become who creates values, not who inherits them.
Eternal recurrence is a thought-weight: would you affirm this life, exactly, forever?
Amor fati — love of fate — crowns the system.
Share this: ask someone if they would relive this week unchanged, forever, and watch the audit begin.

items.title: The Tavern Poet
items.question: Which 13th-century Persian poet wrote of love, wine and the beloved in verses still recited worldwide?
items.correctExplanation: Right — Rumi, whose Masnavi turned divine longing into the world's most translated poetry.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Rumi. Jalaluddin Rumi's verses on love, loss and the tavern of ruin have made him the best-selling poet in America, eight centuries on. The whirling dervishes still dance his order's practice of turning toward the beloved.
items.lessonContent:
Rumi's Masnavi runs thousands of couplets on love as the engine of transformation.
The tavern, the wine, the beloved — every image points past itself.
His order's whirling dance embodies the verses physically.
Translation carries him across eight centuries into airport bookshops.
Share this: read one Rumi couplet aloud tonight and let the tavern do its work.

items.title: Veil of Ignorance
items.question: Which philosopher asked us to design society from behind a veil hiding our own future position in it?
items.correctExplanation: Exactly — John Rawls: justice as fairness, chosen by people who might end up anywhere.
items.incorrectExplanation: The answer is: Rawls. John Rawls's original position — designing society ignorant of your own talents, wealth and luck — yields his two principles: equal liberties first, inequalities only if they help the worst off. It remains the most influential fairness machine in political philosophy.
items.lessonContent:
The veil of ignorance: design the rules not knowing which life you'll draw.
Behind it, rational choosers protect liberties first, then permit only inequalities that help the worst off.
The device converts selfishness into fairness by deleting knowledge of self.
Critics from libertarians to communitarians have taken their best shots.
Share this: redesign one rule in your house from behind the veil tonight.
